newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - Experts see 77-seat margin for UK Labour.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Experts see 77-seat margin for UK Labour.

text.p: Britain's opposition Labour party looks set to form the next government with a 77-seat majority, a Reuters survey of predictions by some of the country's top election experts showed on Wednesday.

The mean prediction from the 20-strong Reuters panel of polling analysts and political scientists is up from an average forecast in March of a 59-seat Labour majority and is the highest prediction since the survey began in October.

The projection showed Labour would oust the ruling Conservative party by winning 367 of the 659 parliamentary seats contested at the May 1 election, with 44 percent of the vote in a first-past-the-post race.

The Conservatives were expected to gather 35 percent and 240 seats and the Liberal Democrats 15 percent and 25 seats. Other parties, including those in Northern Ireland and local parties, were set to gain 27 seats and six percent of the votes.
Panellists said Tony Blair's Labour party had stormed ahead in the two weeks since Prime Minister John Major announced the election date, leaving the sleaze-dogged Conservative party in its wake.

"The first two weeks of the campaign have been dreadful for the Conservative party. Sleaze is at the top of everyone's minds and they have not been able to capitalise on reasonably good economic figures," said Justin Fisher at London Guildhall University.
The panellists said general government competence, including the economy as well as a series of sex and money scandals, would influence voters on May 1.

Personal and political controversies have dominated the headlines over the past week and with just 30 days to go until polling day, the survey showed the odds were stacked against the Conservatives clawing back enough support to regain power.

The Reuters panel was still more cautious than most opinion polls -- its mean forecast put Labour just nine points ahead of the Conservatives, compared with seven points last month, but well behind the gap of around 20 points seen in recent public opinion polls.
The experts had been predicting a last-minute surge in Conservative support, although they said this looked less likely as May 1 drew near.
John Curtice of the University of Strathclyde increased his Labour seat majority projection to 185 seats from 125, but he still believed this was an optimistic forecast for the Conservatives.
"The events of the last two weeks indicate that the Conservatives cannot be relied upon to make a recovery," he said.

Neil Carter of York University agreed: "I based my previous predictions on the assumption that the polls would have narrowed, but they are hardly narrowing at all." He raised his Labour majority to 41 seats from his prediction last month of 11 seats.
The Conservatives received a small consolation from the polls on Wednesday, the day the major parties announced their election manifestos, when a Guardian/ICM poll showed them closing the gap.

The poll put Labour's support at 46 points, down from 48 in March, while support for the Conservatives was up two points to 32. The results were described by the newspaper as a rare ray of hope for the government.

April's survey asked the panel to predict who would be the leader of the Conservative party a year from now. The results were mixed, but John Major could be looking for other employment, with only two of the 18 panellists who gave an answer expecting him to remain leader.

Welsh Secretary William Hague was favoured by three panellists. "He has an ultra-safe seat, he skips a generation and he's not aligned with any major factions in the party. He's a unifying force," said Professor Ivor Crewe of the University of Essex.

Health Secretary Stephen Dorrell, Deputy Prime Minister Michael Heseltine and Home Secretary (Interior Minister) Michael Howard were also seen as possible leadership candidates, with three panellists backing each of them.
